paras: The Caruthersville jail whipping took place at Caruthersville, Missouri, around midnight on March 13-14, 1903, when citizens took three Black men and one Black woman from the jail and whipped them with leather thongs. The four, held on a charge of pilfering during a flood, were then ordered to leave the vicinity. A brief wire dispatch about the whipping ran in papers from Georgia to Arizona, usually as an item in flood news.

In March 1903 Caruthersville was threatened by high water, and a gang of 450 men was working night and day on a new levee behind the old embankment, which the dispatch called "crumbling." Amid this emergency the four, described as "negroes," were accused of "pilfering under cover of the flood excitement" and locked up in jail.

According to the dispatch dated March 14, the four were taken from jail "last midnight" by what most versions called "a posse of citizens." They were whipped with leather thongs and afterward ordered to leave the vicinity. None of the victims or the whippers was named, and no version gives the size of the group or describes the victims' injuries.
No report of arrests, an inquiry or any official response to the whipping appears in the coverage, and the dispatch was not followed up.

The story reached readers only through the white press, as one wire dispatch reprinted between March 15 and March 20 by the Savannah Morning News, the Indianapolis Journal, the Arizona Republican, the Louisville Courier-Journal and the Raleigh News & Observer, and in condensed form by weekly papers in South Dakota and Indiana. Most headlines took the accusation as settled, calling the four "Pilferers," "Negro Thieves" or "Thieves," and the Arizona Republican headed it "Some Negro Men and Women Engaged in Stealing." Only the Indianapolis Journal's "A Flogging Incident" and the Berne Witness's "Whipped by a Mob" named the act rather than the charge, and no paper added comment.

Several papers set the item among reports of levee breaks and flooded towns, so that it read as one more incident of the flood. The South Dakota digest dropped the victims' race altogether, while every fuller version identified them as "negroes." No Black-press report of the whipping was found.

The timing differs among the versions: the March 14 dispatches place the seizure at "last midnight," the Arizona Republican's March 15 text says the four were taken "today," and the Dakota Farmers' Leader says "Saturday night." The March 14 dispatches are the earliest and most specific, and the later datelines appear to be re-filings of the same text.
